text:
It was a vidiprinter moment worthy of a double take. Ross County 1 Cove Rangers 1 (Keir 52). Would Cove, scrapping for survival in Scottish League One, put an unlikely end last Saturday to the most emphatic run in British senior football? Don’t be silly, retorted County; four goals in the closing 17 minutes extended the Dingwall side’s goal difference to plus 45 (for 56, against 11). Played 16, won 14, drawn two. There is as much chance of Mike McCarthy settling down for Christmas dinner with Aaron Rodgers as County missing out on promotion back to Scotland’s second tier. Taking in cup competitions they have scored 102 goals this season.
Assessment from the captain, Brian Graham, of a frankly irrelevant loss on penalties to Stenhousemuir in the Challenge Cup epitomises the County approach. “We should have been five- or six-nil up at half-time,” an irked Graham says. “That shows the standards we have set. We lost a dubious goal, which shouldn’t have stood.” Earlier in that competition County whacked 14 past a Hearts youth side before defeating a Celtic B team including two Chelsea loanees and a £3m midfielder.
Unsurprisingly there is cynicism, laced with jealousy, about County’s position. They are portrayed as wild spenders in a frugal environment. A club in the wrong competitive domain. The analysis does not stack up. Graham, the scorer of 21 goals across all competitions, is 39. The prominent Adam Emslie was last on loan at Cove after being rejected by Aberdeen. Luke McCarvel arrived via Kelty Hearts and Cumbernauld Colts. Lewis Reid is previously of Stranraer, Lewis Strapp a signing from Airdrie. County have a batch of Scottish Championship-capable players, not Premiership-ready ones. Their form is still extraordinary.
“People don’t know the ins and outs of this club,” says Graham. “I speak to the chief executive – as the captain I need to work on the bonuses – and I can see a massive difference now to what it was previously. There’s not players on wages like the exaggeration of what people say they are on. People just play guessing games. But look at Scottish football as a whole; budgets do not give you the right to win matches anyway. It’s players on the pitch who have to do it.
“If you had said to me I would have 21 goals in November, I would have laughed at you. I had a number in my black book which I have exceeded. I now have another number in there.” Not that wider records – 100 goals, 100 points or an unbeaten league campaign – are viewed similarly. “We haven’t spoken about that,” Graham says. “We are getting a lot of plaudits, a lot of people speaking about it, but the manager insists we keep our feet on the ground and don’t listen to outside noise. When you put yourself in the position we have, teams are desperate to beat us.”
Only Boreham Wood, with 16 wins and three draws from 19 National League games and 53 goals scored, are in touching distance of County’s win percentage. Graham is ideally placed to speak on County’s journey. Now in spell three, he played for them in the top flight and when Hibernian were vanquished in the League Cup final of 2016. A club who had been a small Highland League team in the early 1990s were giving bloody noses to the big boys. Subsequent years brought trauma, culminating in successive demotions from 2025. County kept faith in the summer with their manager, Stuart Kettlewell. Graham returned to spearhead a fightback. Pre-season games, which began in late June, included a comprehensive closed-doors win over Aberdeen.
“The manager had to build a new squad and bring in younger players,” Graham says. “The manager has created a new culture that he spoke to me about before I came in. We had to get back to basics, everybody wanting to train every day and fight for their jersey. He has created that environment; nobody is resting on their laurels and everyone is pulling their weight. The manager and coaching staff have really high standards, which the players know about. Nobody gets away with any nonsense.”
The emphasis on attitude is apposite. County have a generous owner and, owing to geographical location, were always known to pay decent salaries to prise players from the central belt. In recent times, received wisdom was that players were using the club for a payday that came free from accountability. The team spiralled as a result, having previously brought wider attention on Dingwall and boosted the local economy.
“It is a community club, a family club,” says Graham. “We have excellent volunteers. One woman comes in every week with her spaniel – I think the dog likes the pies – to help clean the stands but she is not the only one. You want to come to your work because there are good people here.
“At the start of the season the fans were a bit dejected, the numbers weren’t quite there. Slowly but surely people are coming back to support us, they realise this is a team to get behind. It’s a real Ross County side, people willing to fight for the jersey, which is what this club is all about.”
On Saturday County host Brora Rangers in the Scottish Cup. While not quite a derby – the towns are almost 50 miles apart – this is a compelling fixture. Brora look capable of leaping from the Highland League to the Scottish League, as County did in 1994. Graham wants a cup run to bring finance into a business which has had to withstand sharp income drops. There is a more endearing cause. Bobby Wilson, who presided over County’s league entry having scaled European highs when a player with Dundee, died on 18 November. A celebration of Wilson’s life will soon take place at County’s home. He would approve of this resurgence.
digest_he: תחת הנהגתו של המאמן סטיוארט קייטלוול ובכיכובו של החלוץ בן ה-39 בריאן גרהאם, רוס קאונטי רושמת עונה יוצאת דופן לאחר ירידות ליגה רצופות, במטרה לשוב בחזרה לליגה השנייה בסקוטלנד. למרות קולות של ציניות וטענות על תקציבים והוצאות בסביבה תחרותית מצומצמת, המועדון מפגין סטנדרטים גבוהים ועבודה קשה המאפיינת קהילה משפחתית מגובשת. בזמן שהקבוצה מתכוננת למשחק גביע מול ברורא ריינג'רס, היא שואפת להמשיך את המומנטום החיובי ולהנציח את זכרם של אנשי מפתח בעברה.
